title: This AI Just Fixed Google Earth’s Biggest Problem - YouTube

snippets.text: Satellites can see your roof, but not
your front door. These AI researchers
just fixed that problem. Let me explain.
When I worked on Google Maps
photoggramometry, we had this massive
constraint. Satellite-based 3D
reconstructions [music]
were basically useless for anything city
scale. You needed airplanes with these
specialized camera rigs to fly the city
at low altitude. The physics problem is
quite simple. These satellites are
largely looking oblique down or slightly
off native air.
That basically means that you're not
really going to get building facades and
certainly not street level detail. All
that geometry is just oluded, which is
fine if you can fly planes with camera
arrays everywhere, but you can't, right?
Like you've got aerial denied regions,
you've got restricted airspace, you have
conflict zones, huge chunks of planet
Earth are literally unmapped with these
methods, [music] which is why you only
have about 3,000 cities worth of 3D data
inside of Google Earth. These
researchers found a workaround that is
honestly kind of beautiful. They train
Gaussian splats on multi- view satellite
imagery. Basically standard 3D Gaussian
splatting [music] stuff. But naturally,
as the camera descends towards ground
level, the renders completely fall
apart. You've got floating artifacts
everywhere. This geometric nonsense.
[music] Now, instead of trying to fix
this technically, they just leaned into
it. They treat those broken renders as
input into an image diffusion model like
flux and basically say, "Hey, [music]
hallucinate and fill in the missing
parts." That nightmare street level view
becomes a starting point for diffusion
to [music] autocomplete in a sense. But
here's where it gets really clever. They
generate multiple diffusion samples per
view instead of committing to one
solution. That is probably wrong. But if
you generate a couple of versions and
let Gaussian splatting optimization find
consensus across them, you actually get
multiv- view consistency that looks
pretty damn good. They do this
refinement in episodes, this curriculum
style training starting at higher
altitudes and gradually descending.
Hence the name of the paper, Skyfall GS.
[music] So with each iteration, those
ground level views get less screwed up
and more refined. The diffusion model
starts filling in the facades, adding
the texture detail, fixing the
artifacts. By the end, you've got real
time flyable 3D cities that look
surprisingly convincing. [music]
And critically, the geometry still
respects the satellite input. It's not
just making stuff up. It is
intelligently [music] completing
whatever was oluded. No 3D training data
required, no street level photos, no
airplane flyovers, just satellite
diffusion, doing what it does best,
filling in the blanks. This is really
cool because previous methods to do this
type of stuff such as Vicon 3D which
Maxar now owns can suddenly get a huge
boost. In other words, the entire world
including all those aerial denied
regions suddenly became [music]
mappable. That is not just an
incremental improvement. That my friends
is a paradigm shift. Now this is useful
for a lot of different things. There's
actually a program called the US Army
one world terrain program. Essentially,
[music] this is a contract to Knackar to
use satellite imagery across the world
to create this type of synthetic 3D
environment. You know, because the US
military wants 3D data everywhere it
can't necessarily fly airplanes and
drones. But thus far, those 3D
reconstructions kind of look like what
you see in Google Earth. They're kind of
good, great analysis raers, 2 and 1/2D
if you want to figure out the elevation
of something. Not really good to look at
for a human. Certainly not for an AI to
train and figure out how to navigate.
This paper just changed that. It's like
neural scene completion, but actually
practical. And it just unlocked the
whole world. Imagine not just 3,000
cities in Google Earth anymore. Imagine
[music] the entire world.
